item.title: Winning Time: Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces and the New Dimension of War
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth analysis of a significant military development, with clear context and vocabulary for learning.

go beyond the headlines.

November 10, 2026

Oleksiy Honcharuk

In late 2023, Ukraine’s military leadership faced an institutional choice: establish a dedicated branch of the armed forces for unmanned systems or integrate drones into existing branches. Most senior officers I knew opposed the separate force, and their strongest argument was sound within classical doctrine. Each branch of service corresponds to a distinct domain of war: The army fights on land, the navy at sea, the air force in the air. Unmanned systems operate across all of these domains and possess none of their own. No domain, no branch of service. The advocates were mostly newcomers from civilian life, and the opponents were career generals. Within the coordinate system of existing doctrine, the generals were right. The war itself, however, was about to overtake their premise that it unfolds in fixed places. Ukraine created the Unmanned Systems Forces anyway, the first branch of its kind in the world. A force with about 2.5 percent of Ukraine’s military personnel has accounted for roughly a third of Russian losses this past year.

That decision reflected a collision of two cultures. People who entered from civilian life built a different culture: continuous experimentation in place of pre-defined standards and protocols, openness to mistakes as the price of learning, and the habit of improving weapons in combat. For career officers, the question was usually one of means: which systems, in what quantity, and for which branch. The real question lies elsewhere: What game are we playing, and how do we imagine it?

The decisive dimension of the war in Ukraine is not where forces fight, but how fast each side adapts. A unit that updates its tactics and technology every six weeks does not cancel the firepower of a unit that updates once a year — a slower side can still pay in mass, as Russia does. What the faster unit wins is time: It sets the terms of every exchange for as long as the gap lasts. Mass decides how long a side can continue to pay, and speed determines how much each payment buys. I call this the Time Domain: a competition not for territory but for time itself — the interval between the moment a new capability reaches the front and the point at which the enemy’s answer to it works — won by whoever adapts faster. It is also an answer to the generals: The Unmanned Systems Forces do have a battleground of their own — not a place on the map, but a contest, the one their machines are built to win faster than anyone else.

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion, I returned to Ukraine from Stanford to help its fight. I worked inside Aerorozvidka, the volunteer community that pioneered network-centric warfare in Ukraine and helped create the Delta battlefield management system around a single conviction: push battlefield information outward, to those who act on it, instead of holding it inside headquarters. Later, I advised the first commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces and built the team that created the 412th Brigade “Nemesis.”

Throughout this war, Russia has held superiority across every parameter a classical analyst would measure: personnel, artillery, missiles, armor. Under that asymmetry, innovation speed was never an advantage for Ukraine. It was a condition of existence.

The best commanders I worked with understood this intuitively: Tactics had to change faster, commanders had to build units differently, and time was the decisive resource. But they had no language to explain it to headquarters, no metric for a manufacturer, no concept to make it a requirement for doctrine. The analytical apparatus of military thought describes who stands where and how much each side has. It has no category for how quickly a force is becoming something else.

Military doctrine treats a domain as the environment in which operations take place, and NATO recognizes five: land, sea, air, cyberspace, and space. Each answers the question of “where.” But consider an ordinary grass field. People can play football, field hockey, and rugby on the same ground. The ground is identical, yet each game has its own team, its own rules, its own way of winning. The field does not define the game — the rules do. The pattern holds here, too: a distinct game with its own objective and rules, one a force wins on its own terms. Cyberspace earned its spot on the list not because it occupies a physical location, but because the contest there follows a logic the older categories never captured. This is what happened with Ukraine’s drone units. On that shared field, they were playing by rules nobody had written down, and they created a new game: a technology race detached from any portion of space, yet decisive in what happens on the ground. That is the game Ukraine built the Unmanned Systems Forces to play. American author Edward Luttwak described the search for a response as inherent in any military interaction: Adversaries constantly work to reverse each other’s moves. Every advantage has an expiry date. The only question is who renews it first. A single metric judges any decision, whether a commander’s, an engineer’s, or a procurement official’s, by how much time it buys before the enemy adapts.…

Source: War on the Rocks | Published: 2026-11-10 08:30 UTC

Original link: https://warontherocks.com/winning-time-ukraines-unmanned-systems-forces-and-the-new-dimension-of-war/

item.title: To Implement Acquisition Transformation, Empower Military Mavericks
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Technical and strategic insight into military acquisition transformation, with useful vocabulary and context.

go beyond the headlines.

November 10, 2026

Ben McNally and Donald Gansberger

“I wanted disciplined but not regimented thinking. Commanders must encourage intellectual risk-taking to preclude a lethargic environment. Leaders must shelter those challenging nonconformists and mavericks who make institutions uncomfortable; otherwise you wash out innovation.”

— James Mattis & Bing West, Call Sign Chaos

For the last decade, the Pentagon has had the authorities to buy commercially derived technologies at speed and scale, but not enough people who know how to use those authorities. Successive senior Pentagon leaders, both military and civilian, have asserted that these technologies will prove decisive in future wars. Panels, commissions, and directives created new pathways and the Pentagon’s Acquisition Transformation Strategy now makes commercial-first buying a top priority.

This article argues that the Defense Innovation Unit should lead the implementation of this transformation by becoming the department’s weapons school for commercial technology acquisition. Like the Navy and Air Force weapons schools, the unit should select promising servicemembers, train them rigorously, credential them visibly, and ultimately send them back to the services to lead and teach others. Two things make this work: training that turns motivated people into experts and incentives that ensure that time at the unit enhances their careers instead of ending them. The mavericks that built the unit had the first without the second, and many paid for it dearly.

Since 2016, the Defense Innovation Unit has executed hundreds of commercial solutions openings using other transaction agreements through partnerships with limited groups of service personnel whose acquisition knowledge has never scaled. The unit’s experience will be the bedrock of the curriculum.

In November 2014, then-Secretary of Defense Chuck Hagel announced that the Department of Defense was implementing a Third Offset Strategy in response to renewed Russian aggression in Eastern Europe and China’s militarization of the South China Sea. The strategy would “start with a clean sheet of paper” to field several commercially derived technologies, including robotics and autonomous systems. As a part of this strategy, Hagel’s successor, Secretary of Defense Ash Carter, announced that the Pentagon would be establishing a storefront in Silicon Valley called the Defense Innovation Unit Experimental.

In 2016, the unit’s three-person acquisition pathways team constructed a competitive solicitation process called a commercial solutions opening: a-three phase competition emphasizing speed, flexibility, and collaboration in the contracting process by using other transaction agreements, which played a prodigious role in winning the space race and had been re-invigorated by the 2016 National Defense Authorization Act. Using this process made the Pentagon a more appealing customer and leveled the playing field for startups by driving a commercial-friendly approach that recognized startups and their investors’ expectations by providing buy signals at the speed of business, not typical defense acquisition cycles.

From 2016 to 2024, the unit remained separated and secluded from the rest of the Pentagon. The unit had a modest budget, relying on motivated mission partners to fund projects. Servicemembers at the unit were mavericks whose intrinsic motivation to make an impact took precedence over promotion and advancement. They repeatedly warned the rest of the Pentagon about the threat of small drones to parked aircraft, the outsized role of drones in the Nagorno-Karabakh War, and the rapid proliferation of high-quality commercial satellite imagery. Despite complete alignment with the Third Offset Strategy, their warnings were routinely dismissed. While the unit punched well above its weight, it suffered budget cuts and spurious contract award protests. In 2021, Director Mike Brown was nominated to be the Pentagon’s top acquisitions official, only to have his nomination derailed by unsubstantiated accusations of abusing hiring authorities. These events led many at the unit to perceive themselves as rebels resisting bloated Pentagon bureaucracy. Many servicemembers were shuffled back to the services where their careers were negatively impacted. One of us served as the unit’s first warfighter-in-residence, arriving ecstatic at the opportunity to make an impact on capabilities for his community. While many projects worked on were successful, it also meant permanently derailing the author’s military career.

Some of the unit’s most successful projects, including Persistent Maritime Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance, Construction Scale Additive Manufacturing, and Peacetime Indications and Warning, came from coincidental alignment between funded mission problems and solutions from vendors like SailDrone, ICON Technology, Capella Space, and others whose founders hadn’t imagined the military as a customer.

In February 2022, imagery from Capella’s satellites showed the world that Russia was about to invade Ukraine.…

Source: War on the Rocks | Published: 2026-11-10 09:00 UTC

Original link: https://warontherocks.com/cogs-of-war/to-implement-acquisition-transformation-empower-military-mavericks/

Why it is here: Detailed reporting on UK politics with clear analysis and useful vocabulary.

Welcome: Burnham should 'move on' over Brexit, says May

Brexit – or reversing it, 10 years after the event – is the topic dominating the Sunday politics shows this morning after major deals were struck with the EU on Friday on trade, travel, emissions and visas for young people.

Andy Burnham says these are the first steps towards rebuilding “the bridges broken all of those years ago” with “our nearest neighbours and our largest market”.

While he’s voiced support for re-joining the bloc, he’s also stressed that all options are on the table and there’s a long road ahead in convincing the British public and securing the unanimous assent needed from the 27-nation bloc.

Critics have piled in this morning, warning how tricky of an endeavour this could be. Ex-PM Theresa May, whose government was brought down by Brexit in 2019, has told the BBC that the divorce “is done” and he should “move on”.

That interview’s coming up on Laura Kuenssberg’s show later this morning. Meanwhile over on Sky, Brexiteer Michael Gove is hosting Reform and Tory naysayers as well as the European relations minister. I’ll recap their comments.

item.title: ‘Just wrong’: British right distances itself from Trump after Putin ‘friend’ post
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Analysis of political stance with clear context and vocabulary for learning.

Reform UK and the Conservatives have distanced themselves from Donald Trump after the US president posted a photo of himself shaking hands with Vladimir Putin with the caption: “My friend.”

The US president had already used the term to describe the Russian president while at last week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, southern China, where he also met the Chinese president, Xi Jinping.

But the photo with Putin, showing Trump leaning towards the Russian leader to talk to him as they met at the summit, posted by Trump on his Truth Social platform overnight, prompted condemnation in the UK.

Asked for his reaction, Richard Tice, the deputy leader of Reform UK, the British party most closely associated with Trump, replied: “Horror.”

He told Sky News: “It’s just wrong at every level … And it’s a grave mistake. He is not our friend, Putin. He is, as others have said, a murderous dictator. And no one is in any doubt about that.”

Asked whether Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, who is a friend of Trump, would speak to the US president about this, Tice replied: “Oh, there have been a number of occasions where one could agree with Trump, and then disagree with him.

“There have been more occasions recently when clearly we have disagreed with him and said so very explicitly. And in a sense, that’s the nature of long friendships. Sometimes you’ll agree and sometimes you’ll disagree. And, I think the disagreements are growing.”

Reform and the Conservatives under Kemi Badenoch, both of whom welcomed Trump’s re-election in 2024, have increasingly tried to dissociate themselves from the US president amid questions over his temperament and judgment, while his attacks on Iran have driven up global energy prices.

Polling last month for YouGov found that just 10% of British people have a favourable opinion of Trump, with 86% holding an unfavourable view. Asked about the “My friend” post, Alex Burghart, Badenoch’s deputy, said he was “very sad” about it.

He told Sky News: “I’m sad and I’m depressed, because the world that I grew up in was one in which the United States was a defender of freedom. I worry that we might be moving into a world where that isn’t the case any more.”

Asked about his party’s previous support for Trump, Burghart replied: “If you look at what the Conservative party is proposing in terms of defence and foreign policy, it’s very clear that we are still on the side of freedom, and we’re the party that has said that we will put up defence spending to what Nato wants it to be.

“So I think you can trust Kemi Badenoch and the Conservatives on this. But, I very much hope that we don’t enter a world in which large, aggressive powers feel that they can occupy their neighbours and get the approval of the United States.”

When asked about the Trump post, Hamish Falconer, a Foreign Office minister, called Putin “a butcher” and said Andy Burnham would make the UK’s views known.

Falconer told Sky News: “The prime minister speaks to the president regularly and is in absolutely no way pulling his punches about the strength of feeling that the UK has as a whole about Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.”

Source: The Guardian Politics | Published: 2026-11-22 12:36 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/nov/22/british-right-reform-tory-party-distances-itself-from-trump-putin-friend-post

item.title: Voters rejected data centers in dozens of communities, fueling the narrative that opposition to the AI infrastructure contributed to the 2026 blue wave
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Discussion of political trends with useful vocabulary and context.

Data centers were on the ballot, both directly and indirectly, in the 2026 midterm elections.

A total of 41 local ballot initiatives concerning data centers in 10 states were up for a vote. All but one resulted in measures to restrict or limit their development.

The centers also may have played a role in several high-profile contests. In Ohio’s race for a U.S. Senate seat, Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown hammered incumbent Jon Husted for his past support of data centers. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa made Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s track record of supporting tax breaks for data centers a focal point of her winning campaign. Her victory marked a historic break with decades of Republican control in the state. As governor-elect, she immediately reaffirmed her campaign pledge to pursue legislation protecting Texans from data centers.

According to NBC exit poll data, 56% of voters felt that data centers were a major or even a crucial factor in influencing their congressional vote. For Black voters, the share was even higher, at 68%.

Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure, housing the computing resources used to train AI models. These massive facilities guzzle energy and water and are very noisy. Many Americans argue that their costs, in terms of land use, higher utility bills and environmental degradation, outweigh the benefits.

I’m a professor of political science who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of this technology is reshaping established practices and power dynamics in campaigns.

Before the midterms, it had already appeared to be disrupting some partisan alignments. Following those historic elections, which have thoroughly shaken up America’s political geography, the widespread pushback against data centers is now part of the narrative explaining the dramatic results of the 2026 midterms.

Disrupting political polarization

In contrast to many other issues, concern about data centers is relatively bipartisan. The Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans in mid-2026 whether they support or oppose having data centers in their communities. Opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%, but it crossed party lines.

Local ballot measures restricting data centers also cut across traditional political alignments. Communities as disparate as deeply red Edgewater, Florida, and solidly blue Alhambra, California, voted to prohibit them. The margins for the restrictions were large, averaging 49 percentage points.

The one restrictive local measure that failed to pass was in Harwood, North Dakota, population around 800. With a data center project already in progress, political and economic leaders prevailed in arguing that restrictions would cut into local revenue and stifle economic development more generally.

Allies and adversaries

Exit polls taken during the midterm elections also detected a degree of bipartisanship. Of the 56% of voters who said data centers played a “major” or “crucial” role in their vote, approximately two-thirds were Democrats and one-third Republicans. Exit polls, however, should be interpreted with care, given their methodological limitations.

These responses hint at why the narrative that opposition to data centers helped fuel the Democrats’ historic midterm victory emerged right away.

The seeds of this argument were in place before the election, picking up on unusual alliances that marked the data center opposition. In cities and counties, zoning fights are drawing a diverse kind of resistance: environmentalists, voters reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests.

Some of the bipartisanship around this issue has even seeped into Congress. Several weeks before Election Day, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417-3 vote. The bill would require states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs. The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill’s measures, which would be voluntary, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers.

Similar concerns killed the Senate version, a reminder that even allies sometimes follow different strategic paths. Some proponents of tighter regulation will accept incremental progress, while others push for more sweeping change.

Brookings Institution scholars anticipate that the newly elected Congress will take up the issue again, this time with a directive to states to establish mandatory, not voluntary, requirements.

Politics as usual

As the midterm elections approached, candidates up and down the ballot blanketed the airwaves and digital platforms with ads against data centers. President Donald Trump pushed back, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.”

Some Republican candidates walked a fine line between responding to voters’ concerns and not alienating the president.

It matters little whether the data center electoral narrative is accurate, and so far, the reported evidence is limited. We need to know where losing candidates stood on data centers, not just the winners. That voters considered data centers important says nothing about which direction they leaned. And despite a 98% success rate across the 41 local ballot measures, it’s hard to gauge how much resistance there is to the more than 600 proposed data centers that are slated to be built.…

Source: The Conversation Politics | Published: 2026-11-09 13:43 UTC

item.title: Methodology
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Technical report on methodology, with moderate difficulty and less direct relevance to the reader's interests.

This section details how Pew Research Center used data on age, fertility, mortality, migration and religious switching from 201 countries and territories around the world to make estimates of global religious populations in 2020, and to project how those populations will change in the years up to and including 2070.

It uses a question-and-answer format to go through the methods used by Center researchers in the Future of World Religions report.

Q1: How did Pew Research Center estimate baseline figures for 2020?

Q2: How does Pew Research Center’s projection model work?

Q3: How do the results in this study compare with prior Pew Research Center studies?

- The 2015 “Future of World Religions” projections

- The 2017 “Europe’s Growing Muslim Population” projections

- The 2022 “Modeling the Future of Religion in America” projections

Q4: How do you define regions, countries and territories?

This work was a collaboration between researchers at Pew Research Center and the Center for Advanced Studies of Population and Religion (CASPAR) at Krakow University of Economics.

Q1: How did Pew Research Center estimate baseline figures for 2020?

The starting point of a population projection is called a baseline, and in this study the baseline is the year 2020. The demographic methods we used to project populations of religious groups required collecting and standardizing massive amounts of input data about these groups (in each country and territory) for the baseline year, including each group’s population size as well as its age and sex composition. We also needed data for each group (in each country and territory) on patterns of fertility, mortality, migration and religious switching.

The next sections describe how we measured these baseline characteristics.

Estimating religious composition

Using census and survey data information about religious identities, we sorted the global population into seven religious groups: Christians, Muslims, Hindus, Buddhists, Jews, followers of other religions and religiously unaffiliated people. The “other religions” category includes Baha’is, Daoists (also spelled Taoists), Jains, Shintoists, Sikhs, Wiccans, Zoroastrians and many small groups, some of which can be described as folk or traditional religions. The religiously unaffiliated population – sometimes called “nones” – includes people who in surveys and censuses answer a religious affiliation question by saying they do not identify with any religion or that they are atheist or agnostic.

Most of the census and survey data came from questions that measure religion using a direct question like “What is your religion, if any?” The census and survey questions either ask this question by itself, or, less often, they first ask a filter question such as “Do you belong to a religion or religious denomination?”94

It’s worth noting that we rely on how people describe their own religious identity, regardless of whether that identity lines up perfectly with belief or practice. When someone identifies with a particular religious group, we classify them as being part of that group regardless of their beliefs and practices. For example, if someone identifies as Christian, we classify them as Christian whether or not they hold Christian beliefs that may be considered orthodox or attend worship services. Similarly, if someone identifies with no religion, we classify them as religiously unaffiliated even if they hold at least some religious beliefs and attend worship services.

The censuses and surveys we use classify the religious identity of respondents at varying levels of specificity. For example, depending on the source, the most specific level of affiliation measured for a Southern Baptist could be Christian, Protestant, Baptist or Southern Baptist. Researchers coded all religious identities into one of the seven categories used in this study.

Sources used to measure religious composition

The baseline estimates of the 2020 religious population, which we used as the starting point for our projections through 2070, were first published in Pew Research Center’s 2025 report “How the Global Religious Landscape Changed from 2010 to 2020.” That report was based on more than 2,700 data sources, including censuses; large-scale demographic surveys (which often survey more than 10,000 people); general population surveys (which typically survey 1,000 to 3,000 people); information from population registers; the World Religion Database; and government reports.

The vast majority of data underlying the 2020 baseline estimates came from four main types of primary sources: general population surveys; censuses; large-scale demographic surveys; and the World Religion Database.

General population surveys were our primary source to measure the religious composition of an assortment of countries and territories that make up 44% of the world’s population.

Census data was our primary source in countries where 42% of the global population lives. We relied on large-scale demographic surveys, including Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS), as our primary sources for 10% of the world’s people in 2020.

Additionally, we used World Religion Database (WRD) estimates as our primary source in places that are home to 3% of the world’s people. Among the many types of information used to create WRD estimates are statistics gathered from religious communities and assessments from country experts. This type of information is especially valuable for countries like Cuba and North Korea, which have little or no nationally representative census or survey data on religious composition that is publicly available.…

Source: Pew Research Center | Published: 2026-11-18 14:20 UTC

Original link: https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2026/11/18/methodology-future-of-world-religions/
